title: Detect Unsecured Credentials Shared in Chat Messages
shortTitle: Detect Unsecured Credentials Shared in Chat Messages
summary: This detection strategy covers T1552.008, unsecured credentials shared in chat messages, where a user pastes a password, an application programming interface key, a connection string or a private key into a team chat channel instead of a secret store. It matters because chat platforms are backed up, indexed, searchable and often retained for years, and because membership of a channel changes constantly, so a single pasted secret quietly spreads far beyond the people who need it. The telemetry that makes detection possible is data loss prevention or secret scanning output for message content, chat platform audit logs for message creation and file upload, discovery or compliance application programming interface records that expose message bodies, and process telemetry for clients that read chat data or export message history. It fails in practice because chat is genuinely used for code review and configuration discussion, so pattern matching on the words key or password produces heavy noise unless it is combined with entropy checks, channel scope and the presence of real secret formats.

beginner.definition: This detection looks for passwords and secret keys pasted into team chat. Chat is the messaging tool people use at work every day. The rule watches messages and uploads for text that looks like a real secret.
beginner.whyItMatters: Chat messages are stored, copied into backups and searchable later. Anyone who joins the channel can read the old messages. A pasted key often works right away and nobody notices it was shared. Cleaning it up after the fact is hard, because copies already exist.
howItWorks: A content scanning tool reads messages in approved chat channels and looks for secret patterns.
Patterns include long random strings, key headers and connection text that contains a password field.
The platform audit records show who sent the message and in which channel. They also show the time and whether a file was attached.
A secrecy check measures how random the string is, so ordinary words such as password do not raise alerts.
All of this reaches the central log platform, often a SIEM, which means Security Information and Event Management.
A rule scores the finding by pattern strength and channel reach. It then alerts the owner so the secret can be rotated.
beginner.example: Think of a staff noticeboard in a busy corridor. Someone pins a note with the safe combination so a colleague can open the safe later. Hundreds of people walk past, and the note stays there for months. This detection is the person who scans the board each day and removes notes that contain combinations.
takeaways: A chat message is a permanent, widely readable copy of a secret.
Detect the pattern of a real secret, not the word password on its own.
The fix is rotation first, because deletion does not remove existing copies.

objectives: Explain why chat platforms are a high risk location for shared secrets
Name the content, audit and client telemetry that can reveal a pasted credential
Describe how entropy and known key formats reduce false alerts on ordinary discussion
Identify which channels and which secret types deserve the strictest scanning
List the response steps, in order, from containment to rotation to verification
Explain why deleting a message is not sufficient remediation on its own
dataSources: Data loss prevention or secret scanning findings for chat message content with matched pattern type and confidence score
Chat platform audit logs recording message creation, edits, deletions, file uploads, channel membership and private channel creation
Compliance or discovery application programming interface records exposing message bodies for channels in scope
Endpoint process telemetry for chat client binaries that export, archive or bulk read message history
Identity provider logs showing which accounts and external guests hold membership of each channel
logic: The pattern is a chat message or uploaded file whose content matches a strong secret format, such as a private key header, a cloud access key identifier, a bearer token or a connection string carrying an inline password, especially when it appears in a channel with broad or external membership. The fields that must be correlated are the author account, the channel identifier and its member count including guests, the message timestamp and edit history, the matched pattern class and confidence, and any file upload attached to the same message. The benign case is a placeholder value, a documented sample token from vendor documentation, or a variable name discussed in a code review without a real value, so a high entropy string that matches a provider key format inside a general channel following a deployment discussion is what distinguishes the malicious or careless case from ordinary conversation.
pseudoQuery:
# title: Secret Pattern Detected In Chat Message Or Upload
# logsource:
#   product: azure
# detection:
#   selection_pattern:
#     ContentMatchType: ['private_key_header', 'cloud_access_key', 'bearer_token']
#     Confidence: 'high'
#   selection_upload:
#     EventType: 'file_uploaded'
#     Filename|endswith: ['.env', '.pem', '.key', '.yaml']
#   filter_examples:
#     ContentMatchValue|contains: ['EXAMPLE', 'PLACEHOLDER', 'REDACTED']
#   condition: (selection_pattern or selection_upload) and not filter_examples
# level: medium
falsePositives: Engineers discussing a rotated or already revoked key as part of an incident review after the secret was replaced
Documentation and tutorials posted in a channel that contain vendor sample tokens and placeholder values
Configuration file snippets shared for review where the secret field holds a variable reference rather than a value
Connection strings pasted during a live troubleshooting call after the credentials were disabled for the test
tuningNotes: Start in monitoring mode and tune the pattern set until only strong formats alert, then record which patterns your teams use legitimately, such as internal test tokens, and exclude those exact formats. Require a minimum confidence and a minimum channel reach before alerting, and keep the strictest setting for channels with external guests or more than a few dozen members. Scoping to high reach channels means a secret pasted into a small private channel may be missed, so keep a weekly report of all matches for review rather than real time alerting. Always confirm with the secret owner whether rotation already happened before treating a finding as an incident.
